title: Position and Direction Grade 2: Turns, Routes and Direction Words + Free Quiz
meta_title: Position and Direction Grade 2 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach position and direction to Grade 2: left/right, above/below, quarter and half turns, clockwise and route directions. Free quiz plus printables.
excerpt: Left, right, above, below, a quarter turn to the right — the language of position trips up more seven-year-olds than the maths itself. Here is how I teach it, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Stand behind a seven-year-old, point at a shelf and say ‘put the book next to the box, on the left’, and watch what happens. Half the class will freeze. Not because they cannot reach the shelf, but because position and direction at Grade 2 is really a vocabulary problem wearing a maths costume. Left, right, above, below, next to, between, a quarter turn, clockwise — these are words a child has to attach to a physical action before any worksheet makes sense. Get the words solid and the paper questions fall over on their own.

I have taught this topic to a lot of Grade 2 children, and the mistakes are wonderfully predictable. So let me walk through the pieces in the order I actually teach them, with the little traps flagged as we go.

Start with the body, not the book

Before a single worksheet, children need left and right in their own bodies. The honest truth is that most seven-year-olds still mix these up, and that is fine — so do plenty of adults. Pick the hand they write with, name it, and use it as the anchor. ‘Sachin writes with his right hand, so this is right.’

Then play direction games standing up: face the window, take two steps forward, turn to face the door. The word ‘forward’ only means something once the child has moved. This is the counter-intuitive bit parents miss — you cannot teach direction sitting down.

The positional words that matter

  • Left and right — the two that need the most repetition.
  • Above and below — usually the easiest pair.
  • Next to and beside — touching, side by side.
  • Between — something on each side; this one has two neighbours, and children forget the second.
  • In front of and behind — these flip depending on which way a person faces, which is exactly why they are tricky.

Quarter turns and half turns

Turning is where position and direction Grade 2 work starts to feel like maths. A quarter turn is a right angle — the corner of a book. A half turn is two quarter turns, and it leaves you facing the exact opposite way. That last fact is the one worth drilling: after a half turn, forward becomes backward.

Stand the child up and call it out. ‘Face the board. Quarter turn to the right. Now what can you see?’ Do it ten times and the abstract idea of a turn becomes something in the legs, not just on a page. A common slip: children make a full turn when you ask for a half, because spinning all the way round is more fun. Slow them down.

Clockwise and anticlockwise

These two words lean on something fewer children own now — an analogue clock. If there is a round clock with hands anywhere in the house, use it. The hands sweep clockwise; the opposite way is anticlockwise. No clock handy? Trace a big circle in the air with them, starting at the top and going right and down.

Pair turns with direction to build the full instruction: ‘a quarter turn clockwise’ is a complete, unambiguous command. That is genuinely the target skill for the year — combining a size of turn with a direction.

InstructionWhat the child doesEveryday picture
Quarter turn clockwiseTurns right by one right angleMinute hand from 12 to 3
Quarter turn anticlockwiseTurns left by one right angleMinute hand from 12 to 9
Half turnFaces the opposite wayMinute hand from 12 to 6
Full turnEnds facing the startMinute hand all the way round

Following and giving directions on a grid

Once the words are secure, put a simple grid or picture map in front of the child — a park with a pond, a tree and a gate, say — and read out a route: ‘Start at the gate. Go up two squares. Turn right. Go across three squares to the pond.’ The child moves a counter and checks where they land.

Then flip it, which is the harder and more valuable half. You move the counter and the child gives the instructions. Giving directions forces them to choose the words themselves, and that is where you find out whether ‘left’ really stuck. In my experience this reversal is the single most useful five minutes you can spend on the topic.

Up, down, across — not diagonal yet

Keep Grade 2 routes to whole squares along the lines: up, down, left, right. Diagonal moves and coordinates come later. If a child wants to cut across a corner, gently steer them back to counting squares along the grid. Clean habits now save confusion in Grade 3.

A realistic week of practice

You do not need long sessions. Five focused minutes most days beats a marathon on Sunday. A rhythm that works: two days on left/right and positional words, two days on turns and clockwise, one day giving directions along a route, and the weekend for a written worksheet where the child has to read the words cold and pick the answer. That cold reading is where you see what has truly landed.

One honest caveat — do not rush to the abstract. A child who can physically turn a quarter turn to the right is far ahead of one who has only circled the right picture on a page. The body understands direction before the pencil does.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz covering exactly these ideas — positional words, quarter and half turns, clockwise, and following a route. Let your child try it and talk through anything they miss. When they are ready for more written practice, the printable worksheet linked at the end gives graded questions with a full answer key you can print as often as you like.

quiz.title: Grade 2 Position and Direction Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on left and right, above and below, turns, clockwise and following a route. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: A cat sits with a dog on each side of it. Where is the cat?
questions.explanation: Between means there is something on each side. The cat has a dog on its left and a dog on its right, so it is between them.

questions.q: You face the board and make a half turn. What are you facing now?
questions.explanation: A half turn is two quarter turns and leaves you facing the exact opposite way. So you now face away from the board.

questions.q: Which way do the hands of a clock move?
questions.explanation: The hands of a clock sweep clockwise. The opposite direction is called anticlockwise.

questions.q: A book is on the table and a lamp is over it, higher up. Where is the lamp?
questions.explanation: Something higher up is above. The lamp is higher than the book, so the lamp is above the book.

questions.q: How many quarter turns make one half turn?
questions.explanation: A half turn is made of two quarter turns. Four quarter turns would make a full turn.

questions.q: You start at the gate, go up 2 squares, then go right 3 squares. How many squares did you move in total?
questions.explanation: 2 squares up and 3 squares right is 2 + 3 = 5 squares moved altogether.

questions.q: Which turn is the same as a quarter turn to the left?
questions.explanation: Turning to the left goes the opposite way to a clock, so a quarter turn to the left is a quarter turn anticlockwise.

questions.q: Riya faces the door. She makes a full turn. What can she see now?
questions.explanation: A full turn brings you all the way round to face the start. Riya faces the door again.

faq.q: Why does my Grade 2 child keep mixing up left and right?
faq.a: This is completely normal at 6 to 7 — and many adults still pause too. Anchor it to their writing hand and repeat it during everyday moments (which shoe, which side of the plate) rather than only on worksheets.

faq.q: What is the difference between a quarter turn and a half turn?
faq.a: A quarter turn is a single right angle, like the corner of a book. A half turn is two quarter turns and leaves you facing the exact opposite way. Four quarter turns bring you back to the start.

faq.q: How do I explain clockwise and anticlockwise without a clock?
faq.a: Trace a big circle in the air together, starting at the top and moving to the right and down — that is clockwise. The opposite way round is anticlockwise. A round wall clock with hands makes it click fastest.

faq.q: Should Grade 2 children learn grid coordinates yet?
faq.a: Not yet. Keep it to following and giving simple route directions — up, down, left, right along the squares. Coordinates and diagonal moves belong in later grades once the direction words are secure.
